title: Pauri 40, sound: anad sunahu
hookLine: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore

lines: A SONG TURNS TO FACE THE ROOM.
THE LAST PAURI OPENS WITH A CALL.
TODAY: THE SOUND OF THE FORTIETH.
cards: Some songs end by turning to face the room. The singer stops singing about something and starts singing to the people in front of her. Anand Sahib does that in its last pauri.
After thirty-nine stanzas, the fortieth opens with a call: two short words and then a long one, the way you'd call across a crowded hall to get everyone's attention.
You've already learned the sound of the Anand's first pauri. Today, the sound of the fortieth, the one that closes the whole song of bliss.

teach.b: Here's the first line, slowly: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore. Take it in pieces. Anad: a-NUD.
Notice it's not quite anand, the word in the title of the whole song. The Gurmukhi here is written without the nasal sound, anad, a short, open word.
Then sunahu: su-NA-hu, three soft syllables, and it's a call: hear. Then the long one: vaddabhaageeho.
Vadd, with the tongue curled back a little for the d, then bhaa, then gee, then ho: vadd-BHAA-gee-ho. It's a word for a group of people, said as if calling across a room. Then sagal: sa-GAL, all.
Manorath: ma-NO-rath. And poore: POO-re, two beats, the last one light. Put it together: anad sunahu, vaddabhaageeho, sagal manorath poore.

teach.h: SAGAL MANORATH POORE: A LINE THAT LANDS.
teach.b: Two short words like a knock on the door, a long word that opens it, and then a line that lands. Many ragis sing it to a tune that lifts on vaddabhaageeho and settles on poore.
The pauri goes on for five more lines and ends, the way Guru Amar Das ends so many, with the name Nanak and a sound of its own: the unstruck music playing. That's tomorrow.
For today, let the first line get into your mouth. And this is the pauri the sangat sings after the first five at the close of services, so it's a line many Sikhs have sung hundreds of times.

how: At the close of most Sikh services and ceremonies, the sangat sings six pauris of the Anand, the first five and the fortieth, before Ardas; many Sikhs also recite all forty pauris as part of their morning prayers.

o: the great Guru who wrote the whole Anand
you of great fortune, called out to a crowd
a big crowd gathered at the close of service

games.q: the first line, sound by sound — tap the pairs.

s: the six pauris sung at ceremonies are the first six of the Anand
they are the first five and the fortieth, the last.
in pauri forty the opening word is written anad, without the nasal
pauri forty ends with the name Nanak
like so many of Guru Amar Das's pauris.

games.q: the program is ending and the ragis start the six pauris of the Anand. which six are they?
o: pauris one to five, and pauri forty.
games.why: the first five and the very last; together they are sung to close services and ceremonies, and the fortieth is today's.

practice: Say the first line aloud, not perfectly, just aloud, with a pause between the pieces: anad sunahu, vaddabhaageeho, sagal manorath poore.
Say it once more, slower, and listen to your own voice as you'd listen to someone else's; if you know the tune, hum it. Then rest in the quiet it leaves behind, and if you pray, say Waheguru once.

wordCard.voice: Vaddabhaageeho, you of great fortune. The last pauri of the Anand, sung with the first five at the close of Sikh services and ceremonies. It begins: anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho sagal manorath poore.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: anad sunahu, the opening words of the fortieth and last pauri of the Anand.

carryVoice: Your line: anad sunahu. Four hundred days in, the song is still calling. Day four hundred, done.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on the six pauris of Anand at the close of services
